title: In many ways (Hebrews 1:1–4)
hook: God spoke through prophets in many ways, and now by a Son
tomorrow: was Jesus ever really tempted, in a body like ours?

segments.voice: Yesterday, I have finished the race: fought, finished, kept, and then a request for a coat and some books. Yesterday's line: I have kept the faith.
screen: `I HAVE KEPT THE FAITH.` → `A NEW BOOK: HEBREWS.`

segments.voice: Somebody at a dinner table says, God told me to take the job. Half the table nods. The other half goes quiet. Then a cousin mentions a dream that wouldn't let go of her for a week. Does God still speak like that, or has God already said it all? Christians disagree about it, and both sides open to the same page. A new book today, Hebrews, a letter that never names its writer. And its very first sentence is about God speaking.
screen: `GOD TOLD ME TO TAKE THE JOB.` → `HALF NOD, HALF GO QUIET.` → `HEBREWS, LINE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son." Sundry times, divers manners: bit by bit, in many ways. Before, many voices. Now, a Son, "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person." Then one plain act: he purged our sins, and "sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high." Sat down, the way someone does when the work is finished. So which way does all that point? Two views, both inside the faith. Some Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers for example, hear an open door. The God who spoke in many ways still does: a dream, a nudge, a word through a friend. They point to Acts, where Peter quotes the prophet Joel: "your old men shall dream dreams." Other Christians, some in Reformed churches for example, hear a final word. God has spoken in the Son, fully, and the scriptures carry that word; a claimed new message can mislead. They point to the verb itself: hath spoken. Both sides can reach for one test from Paul: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." And both agree on where the sentence lands: in Jesus, they say, the speaking has a face.
screen: `SUNDRY TIMES, DIVERS MANNERS.` · `NOW BY A SON.` · `AN OPEN DOOR: OLD MEN SHALL DREAM.` · `A FINAL WORD: HATH SPOKEN.` · then, large: `GOD HAS SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Listen for a single sound where you are, a fan, a bird, a car, your own breath, and stay with just that one. When another sound or thought cuts in, let it pass and come back to the first. If listening for God is part of your life, this can be that kind of listening too.
In many ways. The first words of Hebrews: God spoke to the fathers by the prophets in many ways, and now by a Son.
Keep this: God has spoken, a tense Christians read two ways, and both start there. Until tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Hebrews says God spoke in many ways and now by a Son. Some Christians hear an open door, others a final word; both test what they hear.

Hebrews.meaning: a New Testament letter that never names its writer

divers.meaning: old English for diverse, of different kinds

Pentecostal.meaning: churches that stress the Spirit's gifts, such as prophecy

Joel.meaning: a prophet of Israel, quoted by Peter in Acts

Reformed.meaning: Protestant churches in the line of John Calvin

notes: Debate shape: two views inside Christianity on whether God still speaks in new ways (continuationist: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, 'for example'; cessationist: 'some in Reformed churches, for example'). Neither ranked; both given their own text (Acts 2:17 / Joel; Hebrews 1:2's 'hath spoken') and a shared test (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). A Keeper should confirm the labels are fair and not over-broad; not every Reformed Christian is a cessationist, and many charismatic Christians also test claims by scripture.
Start of Hebrews. 'A letter that never names its writer' describes the text; confirm wording.
